paragraphs: This paper studies self-attention as a mechanism for learning how entities affect one another. Its examples range from interacting agents to genetic alleles. The central question is whether attention can capture the function governing those relationships, learn it from observations, and apply it to populations or situations beyond those encountered during training.

The authors show that a single layer of linear self-attention can efficiently represent, learn, and generalize functions built from pairwise interactions. Their analysis requires assumptions about the diversity of interaction patterns in the training data, described as minimal. Experiments support the theoretical account, including generalization across population distributions and to out-of-distribution settings.

The paper also introduces two extensions motivated by this view. HyperFeatureAttention learns couplings between different interactions at the feature level. HyperAttention addresses dependencies involving three, four, or more entities together. These contributions connect attention’s representational abilities to the kinds of relationships a task requires, while the main theoretical findings specifically establish capabilities for pairwise interaction functions under the stated assumptions.
icml-2025-a-theoretical-study-of-hyper-s.tldr: The paper explains how linear self-attention can learn pairwise interactions and introduces modules for richer feature and multi-entity dependencies.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how a neural network can acquire a procedure that works beyond the range of examples used to train it. Its case study is a recurrent neural network learning streaming parity, a simple nonlinear sequence task that can be defined for arbitrarily long inputs. This makes sequence length a way to examine extrapolation.

With sufficient finite training experience, the networks undergo a phase transition to perfect generalization across arbitrary lengths. The authors develop an effective theory of how the networks’ internal representations change during learning. They identify a merger of representations that can be interpreted as the construction of a finite automaton implementing the task.

That interpretation gives the result its significance: the learned internal organization supports a repeatable computation, allowing finite training to produce behavior that extends indefinitely. The study presents one mechanism for this kind of algorithm development. Its evidence concerns recurrent networks on streaming parity, rather than establishing that neural networks generally acquire infinitely generalizable algorithms.
icml-2025-algorithm-development-in-neura.tldr: On streaming parity, recurrent networks can transition from finite training experience to perfect arbitrary-length generalization through a representational merger resembling a finite automaton.

paragraphs: AutoCATE addresses the practical work involved in estimating how treatment effects vary with observed characteristics. Although machine learning offers methods for conditional average treatment effect estimation, choosing, tuning, and validating those methods can make adoption difficult. The paper treats those connected decisions as a single automated pipeline selection problem.

The authors formulate this search as counterfactual Combined Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter optimization. In plain language, the system searches over both the estimation approach and its settings within a framework designed for treatment effect estimation. AutoCATE brings evaluation, estimation, and ensembling together, so automation covers the full process described in the paper.

The unified framework also makes it possible to compare different protocols systematically. The authors report that these comparisons yield insights into treatment effect estimation and a final configuration that performs better than commonly used strategies. They release an open-source package to support use and further research. The contribution is an integrated way to organize and automate methodological choices that otherwise require substantial implementation effort.
icml-2025-autocate-end-to-end-automated-.tldr: AutoCATE automates evaluation, estimator selection, tuning, and ensembling for conditional treatment effect estimation in one framework.

paragraphs: This paper aims to generate examples from parts of a data distribution that are poorly represented. Here, minority samples mean instances in low-density regions of the data manifold. Producing such examples can be useful for applications including data augmentation and creative generation, but existing diffusion approaches often use costly guidance specifically designed for that purpose.

Boost-and-Skip changes two parts of the diffusion generation process: it increases the variance of the initialization and skips timesteps. It requires no dedicated minority-generation guidance. The authors support these changes with theoretical analysis and empirical evidence showing that they encourage underrepresented features to appear in generated samples.

The reported experiments show a substantial improvement in minority generation, with results that rival leading guidance-based approaches while using significantly less computation. The significance lies in achieving that behavior through small changes to the generation procedure. The findings support this simpler route to exploring underrepresented regions without asserting that it outperforms guided generation in every setting.
icml-2025-boost-and-skip-a-simple-guidan.tldr: Boost-and-Skip promotes underrepresented diffusion samples through higher-variance initialization and timestep skipping, rivaling guided approaches with less computation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: CLUDI uses diffusion models to tackle clustering: organizing data into groups without supervised class labels. The framework combines diffusion-based generation with features from a pretrained Vision Transformer. Its goal is to use the generative model’s ability to produce variation to help identify structure in high-dimensional data.

Training follows a teacher–student arrangement. The teacher uses stochastic diffusion sampling to generate diverse cluster assignments, and the student learns to turn those varied assignments into stable predictions. Randomness therefore has a specific training role: it provides an augmentation strategy through alternative assignments, giving the student varied signals from which to learn a consistent grouping.

The authors report state-of-the-art unsupervised classification performance across challenging datasets, along with improvements in robustness and adaptability to complex distributions. These empirical findings support the combination of varied teacher outputs and stable student predictions. The methodological contribution is to make diffusion-generated variation part of the clustering learning process, connecting a generative tool with the task of discovering groups.
icml-2025-clustering-via-self-supervised.tldr: CLUDI trains a student to stabilize diffusion-generated cluster assignments, achieving strong reported clustering results with pretrained visual features.

paragraphs: This paper examines when message-passing graph neural networks can make meaningful predictions beyond their training data. Existing theory has made considerable progress on expressiveness, meaning what these networks can distinguish or represent. The authors focus on the separate question of generalization and how it depends on properties of graphs and learning procedures.

They identify three restrictions in existing generalization analyses: graph structure is often overlooked, attention is confined to particular aggregation functions, and the loss is assumed to be the difficult-to-optimize zero–one loss. Their approach extends recent graph similarity theory to examine graph structure, aggregation, and loss functions within the analysis of generalization.

This matters because the resulting account can consider aspects of graph learning that simpler analyses leave out. The paper pairs its theoretical work with an empirical study that supports the theoretical insights. Its contribution is a more detailed understanding of how these ingredients influence generalization, rather than a reported new architecture or a numerical claim about predictive improvements.
icml-2025-covered-forest-fine-grained-ge.tldr: The paper extends graph similarity theory to analyze how graph structure, aggregation, and loss functions influence message-passing networks’ generalization.

paragraphs: Learning a probability density becomes challenging when each example has many coordinates, such as the pixels in an image. This paper shows how deep neural networks can achieve convergence rates independent of the total number of coordinates when the density has an appropriate local dependence structure. The key condition concerns which variables remain dependent after nearby variables are known.

For images, the analysis assumes each pixel is independent of the remaining image once pixels within t steps are given. Under this structure, an L2-minimizing neural network attains the rate n raised to −1/((t+1)²+4). The exponent depends on the neighborhood radius t, which is independent of the total pixel count.

For sequential data with a similar structure, the stated rate is n raised to −1/(t+5). The authors also provide empirical evidence that t is often a small constant in real applications. Together, these results explain how local dependence can make density estimation manageable despite large ambient dimension. The dimension independence is tied to this structural condition.
icml-2025-dimension-independent-rates-fo.tldr: Under local conditional dependence assumptions, neural density estimators can achieve convergence rates governed by neighborhood size rather than total data dimension.

paragraphs: The paper asks what helps vision models understand combinations of concepts beyond those seen during training. It tests the premise that simply increasing data and model scale improves this compositional generalization. Controlled experiments vary the amount of data, the diversity of concepts, and the coverage of combinations, separating factors that can otherwise change together.

The findings identify diversity as the driver of compositional generalization in these experiments. Greater coverage of combinations pushes models toward representations in which concepts have separate additive components. The authors prove that this linearly factored structure enables efficient learning, allowing perfect generalization from only a few observed combinations within their theoretical account.

Tests of pretrained DINO and CLIP models show performance above chance but short of perfect. The authors interpret this as suggesting that the useful representational structure is only partially present. The work therefore motivates attention to which concepts and combinations a dataset contains, and to whether models organize those concepts in a form that supports recombination.
icml-2025-does-data-scaling-lead-to-visu.tldr: Controlled experiments link visual compositional generalization to diverse concept combinations and additive representations, rather than data volume alone.

paragraphs: Sparse networks can reduce parameter counts while retaining strong predictive performance, but fewer parameters do not automatically produce faster computation. Irregularly placed weights can be difficult for modern hardware to exploit. DynaDiag addresses this gap by imposing a diagonal sparsity pattern during dynamic sparse training.

The method preserves sparse computation in both the forward and backward passes. It also uses a custom CUDA kernel built around the diagonal structure, connecting the training design to an implementation that can benefit from that structure. Across diverse neural architectures, the authors report accuracy comparable to unstructured sparse alternatives alongside practical computational gains.

For Vision Transformers with linear layers that are 90% sparse, the reported online inference speedup reaches 3.13 times without sacrificing model performance. Training is 1.59 times faster on a GPU than with equivalent unstructured layers. These measurements illustrate the paper’s central point: a carefully chosen sparsity pattern can preserve the benefits of sparse learning while making the reduced computation useful on hardware.
icml-2025-dynamic-sparse-training-of-dia.tldr: DynaDiag combines diagonal sparse training with a custom CUDA kernel to match unstructured sparsity’s accuracy while delivering measured GPU speedups.

paragraphs: This paper builds interpretability into image classification by controlling which parts of each input remain available for prediction. The method sparsifies images separately for each instance, making the selected visual information part of the classifier’s decision process. The aim is to make predictions understandable through the evidence the model actually uses.

The selection operates over semantically meaningful pixel regions. Learning masks at this level aligns the selected information with human perception more directly than selecting individual pixels. The method also explicitly determines how much sparsity each image requires, allowing the amount of retained information to vary across instances rather than imposing one level on all inputs.

Experiments on semi-synthetic and natural image datasets show more meaningful, human-understandable predictions than the state-of-the-art benchmarks used in the study. The contribution combines two choices: selecting coherent visual regions and adapting the amount selected to the image. Together, they support an inherently interpretable classifier whose prediction process exposes a more understandable subset of its input.
icml-2025-from-pixels-to-perception-inte.tldr: The method makes image predictions more interpretable by selecting meaningful pixel regions and adapting how much information each image retains.

paragraphs: Calibration concerns whether a model’s predictions agree appropriately with observed outcomes. This paper develops a unified Venn and Venn-Abers framework that extends beyond binary classification to prediction tasks specified by general loss functions. It addresses finite-sample reliability, where guarantees that hold only as the dataset becomes arbitrarily large are insufficient.

The construction starts with a predictor that is perfectly calibrated on its own sample and turns it into a set-valued predictor. In finite samples, that set contains at least one marginally calibrated point prediction. The guarantee concerns the presence of such a prediction within the set. Asymptotically, the sets shrink and approach a conditionally calibrated prediction, representing diminishing epistemic uncertainty.

The authors also introduce Venn multicalibration to obtain finite-sample calibration across subpopulations. When the loss is quantile loss, the framework includes group-conditional and multicalibrated conformal prediction as special cases. It additionally produces intervals with quantile-conditional coverage. This connects several reliability goals through one construction while preserving distinctions between set-level, marginal, conditional, and subgroup guarantees.
icml-2025-generalized-venn-and-venn-aber.tldr: A generalized Venn framework produces prediction sets containing a calibrated point in finite samples and connects calibration across tasks, subpopulations, and conformal intervals.

paragraphs: Transformer training can exhibit long periods of little improvement followed by discrete advances. This paper investigates a possible explanation through in-context next-token prediction with n-gram language models. It studies the population cross-entropy loss landscape to understand why solutions corresponding to simpler prediction rules can form plateaus along the learning process.

The authors establish a sufficient condition for parameter configurations to be stationary points. For a simplified transformer, they then construct configurations representing k-gram estimators with k no greater than n. At these configurations, the population-loss gradient approaches zero as both sequence length and parameter norm become infinite. This gives a precise limiting account of near-stationary sub-n-gram solutions.

Numerical experiments support the connection to staged learning, showing discrete transitions between near-stationary solutions. The findings offer a theoretical explanation for why training may pause around partial solutions before progressing. Their force is specific: the stationary-point condition is sufficient, and the vanishing-gradient result uses a simplified model and an infinite-limit argument.
icml-2025-learning-in-context-n-grams-wi.tldr: Simplified transformers have near-stationary solutions representing shorter n-gram rules, offering an explanation for training plateaus and staged progress.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to represent trees, such as hierarchies and taxonomies, in hyperbolic space while preserving their structure faithfully. Such embeddings can also integrate hierarchical knowledge into neural networks. The authors identify two obstacles in existing combinatorial constructions: inadequate separation between points and the computational consequences of needing extra numerical precision.

The first obstacle arises because the construction depends on placing points far apart on a hypersphere, a difficult geometric problem. Poor separation degrades the resulting tree embedding. The proposed highly separated Delaunay tree embeddings incorporate angular separation into a generalized Delaunay formulation, reducing distortion in the embedding.

The second obstacle concerns implementation. Existing use of multiple precision arithmetic prevents practical GPU use in deep learning settings. The authors reformulate the construction with floating point expansion arithmetic, obtaining better embedding quality while retaining compatibility with accelerated hardware. The two contributions address fidelity and usability together: improved geometric placement supports faithful representations, and the arithmetic reformulation makes the required precision compatible with GPU computation.
icml-2025-low-distortion-and-gpu-compati.tldr: Improved angular separation and floating point expansion arithmetic produce lower-distortion hyperbolic tree embeddings that remain usable on GPUs.

paragraphs: Online continual learning requires a model to adapt as the data stream changes, usually without being told where tasks begin or end. Replay methods revisit stored data to help retain earlier knowledge, but they can become unstable after a task shift. This paper develops a second-order optimization account of that instability.

The authors formulate replay learning as joint online optimization with explicit KL-divergence constraints on replay data. Their method, Online Curvature-Aware Replay, uses a K-FAC approximation of the Fisher Information Matrix to precondition gradients. The curvature information stabilizes updates that could cause forgetting while allowing faster optimization along directions that do not interfere with retained knowledge.

The work also adapts Fisher estimation to changing, non-independent data and explains how Tikhonov damping affects the balance between stability and adaptation. On three benchmarks, OCAR outperforms state-of-the-art methods on continual-learning metrics and achieves higher average accuracy throughout training. The results support using curvature to shape updates as the stream changes, alongside the protection supplied by replay.
icml-2025-online-curvature-aware-replay-.tldr: OCAR uses approximate Fisher curvature to stabilize replay-based continual learning and improve average training accuracy on three benchmarks.

paragraphs: Depth prediction networks can be expensive to run on low-end devices. Converting their weights and activations to low-bit representations improves deployment efficiency, but the available precision can be insufficient for depth values spanning a large range. This paper changes the representation of the prediction so that low-precision outputs can still support high-precision depth.

The method encodes depth through two low-dynamic-range components of a two-dimensional Hilbert curve. A full-precision network is trained to predict those components directly. For deployment, standard quantization methods reduce the network’s precision, and an added post-processing step reconstructs depth from the two predicted components.

Experiments report an increase of up to three bits in predicted depth precision with little computational overhead. The authors also observe quantization-error reductions of up to five times. The approach enables accurate depth prediction with eight-bit weights and activations. Its central contribution is to separate the numerical representation used by the network’s outputs from the precision of the final reconstructed depth.
icml-2025-predicting-high-precision-dept.tldr: Encoding depth as two Hilbert-curve components lets quantized networks recover higher-precision depth with little added computation.

paragraphs: Graph learning often has to proceed when some node features are missing. Propagation-based imputation fills those gaps by spreading feature information through the graph. This paper identifies a failure mode in that process: within some feature channels, the resulting values become nearly identical across nodes, leaving little variation useful for the downstream task.

The authors support this low-variance diagnosis with both theoretical proof and empirical evidence. Their proposed remedy injects synthetic features designed to address the cause of the collapse in variation. Propagating these features increases variance in affected channels and helps avoid imputed values that convey essentially the same information for every node.

Experiments cover multiple graph learning tasks and missing-feature rates ranging from low to extremely high. The approach mitigates substantial performance degradation even when missingness is extreme. The contribution is therefore both diagnostic and corrective: it explains why propagated features can lose usefulness and modifies the imputation process to preserve more informative differences between nodes.
icml-2025-propagate-and-inject-revisitin.tldr: Injecting synthetic features counters low-variance collapse in graph feature propagation and mitigates performance loss across missing-feature rates.

paragraphs: This paper analyzes how repeated passes over a dataset affect stochastic gradient descent’s performance on unseen data. In stochastic convex optimization, one pass can achieve optimal excess population loss proportional to one over the square root of the sample size. The authors show that this favorable behavior can deteriorate rapidly in the general nonsmooth setting.

With a step size proportional to one over the square root of n, just a second pass can produce population loss bounded below by a constant. More generally, the stated second-pass-onward loss order combines 1/(ηT) with η√T, where η is the step size and T the total steps. The growing term exposes a tradeoff that additional optimization steps can worsen.

The analysis identifies a change after the first epoch and separates smooth from nonsmooth overfitting behavior. It also extends the asymptotic bounds to sampling with replacement after O(n log n) steps and strengthens a one-pass generalization-gap lower bound. These are theoretical results showing that rapid overfitting can occur, rather than asserting that every repeated-pass run will deteriorate.
icml-2025-rapid-overfitting-of-multi-pas.tldr: In general nonsmooth stochastic convex optimization, a step size optimal for one-pass SGD can lead to substantial overfitting after only one additional pass.

paragraphs: A diffusion model’s output may need to satisfy a downstream objective measured by a reward function. This paper studies how to optimize that reward during inference. Many existing reward-guided methods generate a sample in one progression from a fully noisy state to a denoised result, concentrating optimization into that single generation process.

The proposed framework repeatedly refines a candidate. Each iteration first adds noise and then performs reward-guided denoising. Repeating these two steps allows errors introduced during reward optimization to be corrected gradually. This makes refinement an ongoing process in which the generated result can be revisited through further noising and denoising.

The authors provide a theoretical guarantee for the framework and report superior empirical performance in protein and DNA design. These applications demonstrate the approach in settings where generation is evaluated through downstream design objectives. The contribution is an inference-time optimization framework that uses repeated refinement to improve reward-directed generation, with support from both theory and the reported biological design experiments.
icml-2025-reward-guided-iterative-refine.tldr: Repeated noising and reward-guided denoising let diffusion models refine candidates during inference, with theoretical support and reported gains in protein and DNA design.

paragraphs: SafeArena evaluates whether autonomous web agents comply with deliberately harmful requests. As agents become better at completing website tasks, their capabilities can also enable misuse. The benchmark focuses on that risk by testing agent behavior on concrete web tasks, including both legitimate requests and requests intended to cause harm.

It contains 250 safe tasks and 250 harmful tasks across four websites. Harmful tasks cover misinformation, illegal activity, harassment, cybercrime, and social bias. The authors also introduce an Agent Risk Assessment framework that sorts behavior into four risk levels, providing a systematic way to characterize how agents respond beyond listing individual task outcomes.

The evaluation includes agents based on GPT-4o, Claude-3.5 Sonnet, Qwen-2-VL 72B, and Llama-3.2 90B. GPT-4o and Qwen-2 complete 34.7% and 27.3% of harmful requests, respectively. These benchmark findings show substantial compliance with malicious instructions among tested agents and motivate safety alignment procedures aimed specifically at agents that can act on websites.
icml-2025-safearena-evaluating-the-safet.tldr: SafeArena tests deliberate misuse of web agents and finds substantial harmful-request completion among evaluated systems.

paragraphs: Policy tree search uses a learned policy to guide exploration, with guarantees on search expansions that depend on policy quality. Training that policy commonly requires complete solutions. This creates a difficult starting point: when problems are hard and the policy is randomly initialized, many searches fail before producing the trajectories needed for learning.

The paper proposes learning both subgoals and policies conditioned on those subgoals from the trees expanded during search. Crucially, those trees can come from unsuccessful attempts as well as successful ones. A failed attempt therefore supplies training information even though it does not provide a complete path to a solution.

The authors empirically show improved sample efficiency for learning a policy and heuristic function in this online setting. The approach matters because it makes use of search effort that would otherwise be wasted by training procedures dependent on complete solutions. Its reported benefit is more efficient learning from the search process, particularly addressing the costly early stage when solving hard instances is still difficult.
icml-2025-subgoal-guided-policy-heuristi.tldr: Learning subgoals and subgoal-conditioned policies from expanded search trees, including failed attempts, improves online policy and heuristic sample efficiency.

paragraphs: This paper asks whether transformers can learn causal rules from demonstrations and apply them to new graph structures. Because interventional data is costly, the authors study passive training examples that illustrate an axiom. The specific task is to determine whether one variable causes another when the causal graph structure is already supplied.

Their axiomatic training scheme teaches a 67-million-parameter transformer using linear causal chains and some noisy variations. The model generalizes well to longer chains, reversed chain order, and branching graphs, even though those settings were not explicitly included in its training. The results indicate that demonstrations can support transfer of a causal rule across different graph forms.

On the studied task, the model performs comparably to or better than many larger language models, including GPT-4, Gemini Pro, and Phi-3. The framework offers a way to learn reasoning rules through examples, with potential application to arbitrary axioms when enough demonstrations can be generated. The demonstrated generalization concerns reasoning from supplied causal structures.
icml-2025-teaching-transformers-causal-r.tldr: A transformer trained on demonstrations of causal axioms generalizes from simple chains to unfamiliar graph structures on a causal-relation reasoning task.

paragraphs: In bandit pure exploration, an algorithm samples uncertain options to answer a question about their distributions with a prescribed level of confidence. It should reach the correct answer using as few observations as possible. This paper studies batched algorithms, whose sampling choices can change only between groups of observations.

Batching introduces a second resource to analyze: how often the algorithm must revise its sampling behavior. The authors establish an instance-dependent lower bound on the number of batches required by any sample-efficient algorithm for any pure exploration task. The qualification matters because the bound concerns algorithms that also use observations efficiently.

They then propose a general batched algorithm and prove upper bounds on its expected sample complexity and batch complexity. Best-arm identification and thresholding bandits illustrate both sides of the analysis. Together, the results characterize limits and achievable guarantees for balancing the number of observations with opportunities to adapt sampling decisions, making the cost of restricted adaptivity explicit.
icml-2025-the-batch-complexity-of-bandit.tldr: The paper bounds how many batches sample-efficient bandit exploration requires and provides a general algorithm with sample and batch complexity guarantees.

paragraphs: Standard analyses of gradient descent often assume that a single constant bounds the objective’s curvature everywhere. Under this smoothness assumption, minimizing a quadratic upper bound leads to a step size equal to the reciprocal of that constant. This paper asks how the same reasoning can extend when curvature is bounded more flexibly.

The authors assume the Hessian norm is bounded by a function ℓ of the gradient norm. They derive a gradient descent step size by integrating the reciprocal of ℓ over gradient-norm arguments ranging from the current norm to twice that norm. The rule therefore links the step size to the generalized curvature bound and the current gradient.

Using this rule, the paper improves existing theoretical convergence rates and obtains results in previously unexplored settings. The analysis covers both convex and nonconvex objectives. Its contribution is a principled step-size construction under the stated generalized smoothness assumption, extending the familiar connection between an upper bound on the objective and a justified gradient descent update.
icml-2025-toward-a-unified-theory-of-gra.tldr: A gradient-dependent step-size rule extends gradient descent theory to generalized smoothness and improves stated convergence guarantees.

paragraphs: Strong sequence prediction can suggest that a foundation model has learned the deeper system generating its data, but evaluating that possibility is difficult. This paper introduces an inductive bias probe: a technique that examines how a model adapts to synthetic datasets produced by a proposed world model.

The probe asks whether the foundation model’s tendencies during adaptation align with that underlying model. This shifts evaluation toward what the model carries into new tasks. Across multiple domains, the authors find that models can perform very well on their training tasks while failing to acquire an inductive bias toward the proposed world model.

In the orbital-trajectory study, trained models consistently fail to apply Newtonian mechanics when adapted to new physics tasks. Further analysis suggests behavior consistent with task-specific heuristics that do not transfer. These findings show why success on a prediction task alone may provide insufficient evidence of deeper understanding, and the probe supplies a way to investigate that distinction through adaptation.
icml-2025-what-has-a-foundation-model-fo.tldr: Inductive bias probes show that strong training-task performance can coexist with failure to transfer an underlying world model to new tasks.

paragraphs: Machine unlearning seeks to remove selected training examples’ influence more cheaply than retraining a model. This paper studies when that computational advantage is possible. It establishes upper and lower bounds on minimax computation time, comparing the best available algorithm against the most difficult objective within the problem setting.

The analysis concerns strongly convex objectives and assumes that the unlearning method cannot access the data to be forgotten. The authors introduce an unlearning complexity ratio comparing the computational cost of the best unlearning method with full retraining. A phase diagram organizes how this ratio changes across the analyzed conditions.

The diagram has three regimes: reduced-cost unlearning is infeasible, adding noise alone suffices, or unlearning offers substantial computational savings. Data dimension, the number of examples to forget, and privacy constraints help determine the regime. The result makes clear that efficient removal depends on the problem’s parameters, with the conclusions grounded in the stated objective class and lack of access to forgotten data.
icml-2025-when-to-forget-complexity-trad.tldr: For strongly convex objectives without access to forgotten data, the paper identifies when unlearning is cheaper than retraining, trivial through noise, or computationally infeasible at reduced cost.
